paras: The killing of Jim Torney was the reported killing of a Black farm laborer by a crowd of white men near Pell City, Alabama, in July 1888, after he eloped with Maude Broyles, the sixteen-year-old white daughter of his employer. Birmingham dispatches said the pursuers recovered the girl and were believed to have killed Torney and thrown his body into the Coosa River, though no report said a body was found. The story broke the same week as the lynching of Frank Stone at Pell City, and a national news digest joined the two cases in a single sentence.

According to a Birmingham special to the Atlanta Constitution, Torney was "a negro laborer" on the farm of John Broyles, described as a well-to-do farmer near Pell City, whose daughter Maude was sixteen. His name was spelled differently from paper to paper: Jim Forney in the Memphis Appeal, Jim or James Torney in the Constitution and the Belmont Chronicle, and James Farney in a syndicated summary.

The Constitution's dispatch, dated Birmingham, July 13, and based on a special from Pell City that night, said the couple had eloped "yesterday" and that a crowd of white men set out after them as soon as the affair became known. The pursuers overtook the pair on Trout Creek mountain near Greenport, where, by this account, the girl "turned and fought her captors with the fury of a tigress." In the confusion Torney got away, but several of the party went after him, and the dispatch said "it is believed" he was captured, killed and thrown into the Coosa River.

The Memphis Appeal's shorter Birmingham special, printed on July 14, was just as tentative, saying only that the pursuing party, "it is said, killed the negro." Both dispatches said the girl was returned to her parents.
No report of a recovered body, an inquest, arrests or a prosecution appears in the coverage.

The Memphis Appeal printed the elopement among its "Brief Telegrams" on July 14, two items below a separate Birmingham report that Frank Stone had been lynched "at Bell City" for an outrage on a white woman. Three days later the Atlanta Constitution gave the story its own headline, "She Eloped with a Negro," with a deck saying a mob had pursued them, "Killing the Negro and Returning the Girl to Her Home," although the dispatch below it reported the killing only as a belief. Its account dwelt as much on the girl's resistance to her captors as on Torney's fate.

A syndicated weekly news summary, carried in Dakota and Wisconsin papers, dated both Pell City cases to the 14th and stated without qualification that "James Farney (colored) met a like fate" to Stone "for eloping with a little colored girl." The only comment found came from the Belmont Chronicle of St. Clairsville, Ohio, which said the couple had shown "bad taste" and "but little sense" but that this was "no sufficient reason" for "a crowd of bloodthirsty whites" to "brutally murder poor Torney." The Chronicle closed with the sarcastic remark that the crowd had once more "vindicated the superiority of the white race."

Accounts differ on the girl's race: the two Birmingham specials and the Belmont Chronicle described Maude Broyles as white, while the syndicated summary called the girl "little" and "colored" and did not name her. The Birmingham dispatches are closer to the event and give the names of the girl and her father, while the summary is a condensed national digest. The reports also differ on certainty, since the originating dispatches gave the killing as rumor and the later digest and Ohio editorial stated it as fact. The digest's date of the 14th is also later than the Constitution's account, which put the elopement on July 12 and its outcome in a report on the night of July 13.

reader.title: Killing of Jim Torney
bases: A crowd of white men pursued a Black laborer who had eloped with his employer's white daughter and were reported to have killed him and thrown his body in the Coosa river (A1, A4).

A 'crowd of white men' with no legal authority chased Torney for eloping with a white girl, and 'several of the party' were reported to have killed him (A4); the Birmingham dispatches give the killing only as rumor ('it is said', 'it is believed') and no body was reported found (A1, A4), though later papers state it as fact (A8, A10).

Two separate Birmingham specials, to the Memphis Appeal and the Atlanta Constitution, agree on the elopement, the pursuit and the reported killing (A1, A4), but both hedge on the killing and a syndicated summary differs on the girl's race (A8).

accounts.label: Birmingham specials (from Pell City)
accounts.gist: Maude Broyles eloped with Torney; a crowd of white men overtook them; Torney escaped but was believed captured and killed and thrown into the Coosa; the girl was returned home.

accounts.label: Syndicated news summary
accounts.gist: On the 14th James Farney 'met a like fate' to Frank Stone, lynched for eloping with 'a little colored girl'.

accounts.label: Belmont Chronicle editorial
accounts.gist: Treats the murder as fact and condemns the white crowd for it.

framing.detail: Memphis Appeal ran the elopement as a two-sentence brief telegram below the Stone lynching, with the killing as 'it is said'.

Atlanta Constitution headlined 'She Eloped with a Negro' and stated the mob was 'Killing the Negro', though its text reports only a belief; it dwells on the girl fighting 'with the fury of a tigress'.
Syndicated summary paired Farney with Stone as having 'met a like fate', with no comment.
Belmont Chronicle called the pursuers 'bloodthirsty whites' who 'brutally murder[ed] poor Torney' and mocked their claim of white superiority.

conflicts.note: No paper uses 'Ferney'; Torney is the spelling in the fullest dispatch.

versions.value: white (Maude Broyles, daughter of John Broyles)

conflicts.note: The two Birmingham specials are closer to the event, name the girl and her father, and agree; the summary is a condensed national digest.
The later, distant reports add certainty that the originating dispatches do not have.
The Appeal printed the report on July 14 (A1), so the 14th is likely a digest date.
